title: Departure from Sinai and Wilderness Complaints

date.label: Narrative date: 20th day, 2nd month, 2nd year (Num 10:11)
date.note: Numbers 10:11 dates the departure from Sinai within the biblical narrative to the 20th day of the 2nd month of the 2nd year. That narrative date is not independently established as an absolute BCE date; no absolute year is inferred.

claims.claim: The received Numbers narrative contains the departure from Sinai and wilderness complaints material across Numbers 10–12.
claims.evidence: Numbers 10:11–12:16; biblical-text description, not independent evidence for an event date.

claims.claim: The exact archaeological or external historical setting of this entire passage has not been independently established.
claims.evidence: Phase 2 Dossier 3: the complaint, quail, seventy-elders, Eldad and Medad, and Miriam/Aaron episodes are literary and theological material rather than archaeologically recoverable history, and claims about a historical mass quail event, Taberah, or Kibroth-hattaavah remain Unknown externally. QA Phase 4 §5.3 concurs (quail/Taberah/Kibroth-hattaavah treated as Unknown; no scholarly source named in the dossier).

claims.claim: Comparisons with related biblical laws and retellings need to preserve differences in wording, chronology, or institutional setting.
claims.evidence: Internal textual comparisons documented in CONNECTION-AUDIT.md; interpretation of literary relationship, not an archaeological observation.

connections.note: Poetic remembrance of wilderness complaints and food.

Moses’s retrospective retelling of the leadership burden and appointment of judges; “I am not able to bear you myself alone” (1:9) closely parallels Num 11:14, 17, though the traditions differ in setting and detail.
Poetic retelling of wilderness craving and divine response (cf. Num 11).
Names Moses, Aaron, and Miriam together as leaders sent before Israel.
“Let God arise” echoes the ark saying of Num 10:35; direct literary dependence is not demonstrable from wording alone.
Paul’s typological reading of the wilderness generation as examples and admonition; explicit theological reception, not independent historical corroboration.
